## TL;DR

Worktree cleanup is now automatic and fail-closed. The boot/close-out sweep
reclaims only worktrees RepoOS can prove redundant with main, reports every
retained entry with an actionable reason, and lists worktrees outside its
managed directory as external and untouched. The final review round found one
blocking scope violation — a generated engineering-report JSON committed under
`work/engineering-reports/` — which I dropped, leaving the branch touching only
this task's own task file plus source, tests and docs.

## Work and rationale

The core decision was to make `sweepStaleWorktrees` the single policy shared by
boot, close-out, `repoos gc`, `repoos gc --dry-run`, and `repoos status`.
Because they all call the same function with the same inputs, candidate,
retained and external counts cannot drift between the CLI and the status view;
the tests assert that agreement directly.

Eligibility is proven, never inferred from metadata. A task is *resolved* only
when it is `done`, or archived **and** AI-assigned; archived-but-ready and
human-assigned tasks stay retained. For a resolved task the sweep first tries
ancestry, then a content proof that compares the branch tip against main over
the paths the branch touched. A recorded `merged_commit` lets the proof skip
commits that already shipped, so WIP self-check checkpoints are reclaimable,
while later divergence in main keeps the branch. Non-ancestor branches proven by
content are deleted with `-D`; dry-run reports the same deletion.

Dirty `work/*.md` files do not block cleanup by path alone. The sweep compares
each dirty task file's working-tree bytes with main's canonical copy and
reclaims only exact matches or deletions; unique task data retains the
worktree. That mirrors the merge path's "main's task file wins" rule, applied
only after a byte comparison.

Ignored files needed explicit handling because `git status` hides them. The
sweep inspects them and keeps a worktree holding a local `.env`, attachment
tree, or scratch data; only a scoped allowlist of regenerable output (root
`dist`/`coverage`/cache, `node_modules`, VitePress build paths) may be
discarded. An inherited `.env` symlink into the canonical checkout is the one
safe exception, and an unresolvable symlink is an inspection failure that
retains.

## Approaches tried

The early sweep was `integrate-only`, which is why the 2026-11-01 residue
accumulated. I replaced that with a full safe sweep gated on the task index and
durable close-out records, and made unreadable state skip cleanup rather than
treat everything as inactive. I also tried a path-shape check for ignored
output; review found nested `dist`/`coverage`/`.repoos` could be tracked source,
so I narrowed it to exact root locations and stopped discarding tracked dirty
files by shape at all.

## Challenges and blockers

The hard part was distinguishing "provably absent" from "could not inspect".
`existsSync` collapses EACCES, EIO and ELOOP to `false`, which could force a
removal after a transient error. I replaced those decisions with explicit
`lstat`/`realpath` presence states and separated an absent blob from an
unreadable one using `ls-tree` followed by `cat-file`, surfacing inspection
failures as `could not inspect branch content`. Close-out records and the task
index are similarly fail-closed: unreadable means skip the whole sweep.

The only blocker this round was the out-of-scope generated report file. Removing
it restored the task-scope rule; the stale task-file diff versus main is
bookkeeping that close-out resolves by taking main's copy.

## Key learnings

A cleanup rule is only safe if it can name the evidence. Ancestry, byte
equality, and a content diff are evidence; task status, archive flags, and path
shape are not. Fail-closed inspection matters as much as the eligibility rule,
because a transient filesystem error that reads as "missing" is a data-loss
path. Finally, one shared sweep function is what keeps the operator-facing
counts honest.
